Gloss: The Sun is son of the Titan Hyperion; Ovid names the race for the individual.
Sense: Used in a run of gods named before they exist — there is not yet a sun to be a god of.

Gloss: Greek Phoibē, feminine of Phoibos; also a standard name for the moon.
Sense: At 12 the word does duty for the moon itself, before there is a goddess to bear it.

Gloss: A sea-goddess, wife of Neptune; her waves are simply the sea.
Latin deus et melior natura.
Sense: Ovid never settles whether the world was made by a god or by nature, and never supplies a name.

Epithet: he — whichever of the gods he was
Gloss: Latin quisquis fuit ille deorum.
Sense: The refusal to name is deliberate. Compare the precision lavished on four walk-on river gods at 579–80.

Gloss: Latin dei... vis.
Latin fabricator.
Greek name of the east wind. Ovid gives it no Latin alternative.
Greek name of the west wind.
Sense: Also used as a plural common noun, “the Zephyrs” (108), for spring breezes generally.

Gloss: Greek name of the north wind.
Latin name of the south wind.
Latin opifex rerum, “maker of things.”
Sense: Same root as the title Apollo gives himself at 523, Aid-Bearer (opifer).

Gloss: Iapetus is a Titan; the son is Prometheus.
Sense: Named only by his father at the moment he makes humankind. The translator's own footnote has to supply “Prometheus.”

Gloss: Latin Tellus / Terra, personified.
From Iovis, the oblique stem of Iuppiter.
The nominative Latin name.
Goddess of grain; the phrase means simply grain.
Sense: The first sowing in the poem is dated by the goddess's name rather than the crop's.

Gloss: The last divinity to abandon the earth.
Sense: The Iron Age is defined by her departure rather than by anything men do.

Gloss: Latin virgo Astraea, the Star-Maiden — Justice personified.
Latin Gigantas.
Latin pater omnipotens.
Sense: Kept for the Gigantomachy, where he is nothing but force.

Gloss: The Giants were born from her.
Latin Saturnius. Saturn is the father he deposed.
Sense: Chosen for the line where he first looks down on Lycaon: the son who overthrew his father, about to destroy his own creation.

Gloss: Latin Tonans, an actual cult title at Rome.
Sense: Applied to his house rather than his person — gods travel the Milky Way to the Thunderer's address.

Gloss: Latin sceptro... eburno.
Sense: The council of gods is staged as a session of the Roman senate, and its president is described by his regalia.

Gloss: Latin anguipedum, “the snake-footed” — the Giants of 152, each preparing to throw a hundred arms at the sky.
Sense: Jove is recalling the revolt Ovid has just narrated, but describes it as though it were another one. The translator's footnote has to confirm they are the same.

Gloss: An old sea-god; his name stands for Ocean.
Sense: Jove swears to destroy everything the sea encircles, and names the sea by a god who appears nowhere else in the poem.

Epithet: the lord of gods and storms
Gloss: Jove's phrase for himself, in council.
Arcadia is his kingdom.
Sense: Jove withholds the name through the whole approach to the house, though he has used it twice already in council.

Gloss: Latin Erinys; the goddesses of vengeance standing in for the state they cause.
Sense: “Where lies the land, the Furies rule these beasts” — the crime is named by its goddess.

Gloss: Latin rex superum.
The thunderbolt, named by the smiths who forged it.
Sense: Jove sets the bolt down, and the epithet turns his weapon back into an object somebody had to make.

Gloss: Latin name of the north wind — the same god as Boreas.
Sense: Ovid uses the Greek name once and the Latin name twice, for one god, without signalling the switch.

Gloss: Greek name of the south wind — the same god as Auster.
Sense: The flood is loosed by Notus and dismissed by Aquilo: Greek name in, Latin name out.

Gloss: The Latin name.
Latin nuntia Iunonis; the rainbow is both her office and her dress.
Latin caeruleus frater.
Sense: He is given a colour and a relation before he is given a name. The name arrives eight lines later, with the trident.

Gloss: The Latin name.
Titaness of divine law.
Latin quae tunc oracla tenebat, “who at that time held the oracles.”
Sense: Themis, not Apollo. She held Delphi before he took it, and the word doing the work is “then.”

Gloss: Latin Sol.

Sense: Deucalion wishes he could remake humanity “with my father's skill” — the thing Prometheus is for.

Gloss: A vocative in prayer.
Themis' riddle: the “great mother” is the Earth, and her bones are stones.
Sense: Pyrrha reads it literally and refuses. The epithet is a puzzle before it is a name.

Gloss: Son of the Titan who made humankind.
Sense: Used at the moment he works out how to remake humankind — the son solving his father's problem.

Gloss: Epimetheus is Prometheus' brother, so she and Deucalion are cousins.
Deucalion's solution to the riddle.
Granddaughter of the Titan Iapetus.
Sense: Her one grand name arrives on the line where she hesitates and does not act.

Gloss: Latin septemfluus — the seven mouths of the delta.

Sense: Addressed in the second person: “Against her will, she bore you then.”

Gloss: Latin deus arcitenens, “bow-holder.”
Sense: Named by the weapon he is about to mock Cupid for carrying.

Gloss: Latin superati... serpentis; the Pythian games take their name from it.
Greek Phoibos, “bright, radiant.”
Sense: Also the Sun's name at 752, and Ovid never disambiguates.

Gloss: Greek daphnē, “laurel.”
Sense: She carries the name of what she becomes from her first line.

Gloss: Latin Cupido, “desire.”
Latin Delius; born on Delos.
Latin puer, “boy.”
Sense: Apollo's word for him, and the reason he underestimates him.

Gloss: Latin Veneris filius.
Sense: His answer to being called a boy.

Gloss: Daughter of the river Peneus.
The Greek name; used once in Book 1.
Sense: It appears only for the bone Cupid's arrow passes through.

Gloss: God of weddings; the name stands for marriage itself.
The Latin name.
Jupiter granted Diana perpetual virginity.
Sense: Daphne's precedent for the request she makes of her own father. He enters the episode as a guarantor of chastity a hundred lines before he takes Io by force.
Apollo calls her by her father — the father she will call on to destroy her shape.

Epithet: lord of Delphi, Patara, Tenedos and Claros
Gloss: His four oracular seats.
Sense: Recited to a woman who is running away from him.

Gloss: Latin opifer, “help-bringer” — Apollo as god of medicine.
Sense: Given by Apollo to himself, in the sentence where he admits no herb cures love.

Gloss: Latin Amor.
Sense: In the chase the god shrinks to the force he personifies: “Love's wings proved faster.”

Gloss: A river of Thessaly, and Daphne's father.
Latin laurus, the tree she becomes.
Sense: Apollo names the tree, and the name turns out to have been hers all along.

Gloss: Greek Paian, the healer; also the name of a hymn.
Sense: The healer's title, in the line after the healing fails.

Gloss: Latin magni... amnis.
Latin populifer — a Thessalian river lined with poplars.
Sense: Four rivers, one stock adjective apiece, in two lines: the Homeric catalogue manner, compressed.

Gloss: Latin Apidanusque senex.
Latin placidus.
Latin Enipeus ferox.
A river of Argos, and Io's father.
Sense: His grief carries the book's hardest line about divinity: “To be a god is pain: death's doors are shut” (662).

Epithet: him who wields Heaven's scepter and who hurls its wandering bolts
Gloss: Jove introducing himself to Io.
Sense: Two lines of self-description in place of a name, offered as reassurance, immediately before the rape.

Gloss: Latin Inachis.
Sense: She is turned into a cow in the same line that names her by her father.

Gloss: Daughter of Saturn — the same descent as Jove.
Sense: Ovid's name for her whenever she is out-manoeuvring her husband. Her claim on the throne is exactly as good as his.

Gloss: Latin soror et coniunx: Juno is both.
Sense: Produced at the moment Jove cannot refuse her the cow. The double claim is why he loses.

Gloss: Latin Arestoridae.
Latin stellatus, “starred.”
Sense: The same idea does his hundred eyes and, at 722, the peacock's tail they become.

Gloss: Latin caelestum rector.
Sister of Phoroneus, an early king of Argos.
Sense: The rarest name in Book 1, and it lands on the line where Jupiter finally decides to help her.

Gloss: Son of Maia, one of the Pleiades.
Sense: A constellation standing in for a mother.

Gloss: Latin Atlantiades; Maia's father is the Titan Atlas.
Greek syrinx, “pan-pipe.”
Ortygia, an older name for Delos, her birthplace.
Sense: Pairs with Apollo's “the Delian lord” (455): the twins get one island under two names.

Gloss: Daughter of Latona (Greek Leto).
A water nymph.
Pan gives the reeds her name, and syrinx becomes the word for the instrument.
Sense: She is never named again; the name goes to the object. Compare Daphne and “Laurel” (559).

Gloss: Born on Mount Cyllene in Arcadia.
Sense: Ovid saves the most formal name for the line where he draws the sword.

Gloss: The madness Juno inflicts on Io.
Latin paelex Argolica, “the Argive concubine.”
Sense: Juno's term for her. There is no person in it.
Ovid breaks off to address the river directly, at the end of Io's flight.

Gloss: Io ends as the Egyptian goddess Isis, whose priests wore linen.
Sense: The last transformation is a change of cult, not of body — and Ovid never writes “Isis.”

Gloss: Latin creditur, “is believed to be.”
Sense: Ovid hedges the parentage in the same breath he asserts it — which is precisely what Epaphus will not allow Phaëthon to do.

Gloss: Latin Sole satus.
Sense: The claim the whole quarrel is about, asserted by the narrator before anyone proves it.

Gloss: Greek Phoibos, “radiant” — shared with Apollo.
Sense: The one epithet in Book 1 with two owners. Phaëthon boasts that Phoebus is his father; three hundred lines earlier the same word meant Apollo. The quarrel with Epaphus turns on a name that will not resolve.

Gloss: Latin Inachides; Io's son, so Inachus' grandson.
Clymene, now married to King Merops of Aethiopia.
Clymene's oath, sworn on the sun without naming him.
Latin Sol.
A Roman cult name for Vulcan, from mulcere, “to soften” (metal).
Sense: Ovid names the smith-god by his trade, on the doors that are his work.

Gloss: Latin canorus; his conch is his instrument.
Latin ambiguus — the sea-god who holds no single shape.
Sense: An epithet that is also a plot summary, and in this poem a signature.

Gloss: Sea-nymphs; Doris is their mother, Nereus their father.
Latin Clymeneia proles.
Sense: Named by the mother whose word is the only evidence he has.

Gloss: Latin creditus, “believed.”
Sense: The doubt is built into the epithet, in the line where he arrives to settle it.

Gloss: Greek Phoibos, “radiant”; shared with Apollo.
Sense: In Book 2 the ambiguity of 1.752 is fully exploited — Phoebus is the Sun here and Apollo at 545.

Gloss: Latin non negandus.
Sense: The father settles in half a line what the boy crossed the world to ask.

Epithet: O shared light of the wide world
Gloss: Latin lux publica mundi.
Sense: Phaethon claims a private father by naming him public property.

Epithet: who hurls fierce thunder with his fearful hand
Sense: The Sun ranks himself above Jove by the one thing Jove cannot do: drive this chariot.

Gloss: From Iovis, the oblique stem of Iuppiter.
A sea-goddess, wife of Ocean; Clymene's mother, so Phaethon's grandmother.
The constellation, named by the bull's part that matters to a driver.
Sense: Ovid gives the zodiac as a bestiary rather than a set of signs — the sky is a road through animals.

Gloss: The constellation Sagittarius, identified with the Thessalian centaur.
Latin vigil Aurora.
Latin Lucifer, the last star to quit the sky.
Sense: Ovid makes the morning star the commander of a retreat.

Gloss: The Sun is son of the Titan Hyperion; the race stands for the individual.
Sense: The same name as at 1.11 — where there was not yet a sun for it to mean.

Gloss: Ursa Major and Minor, which never set.
The constellation Draco, by the icy pole.
The constellation Ara.
The goddess standing in for the outcome.
Sense: The Sun's last word of advice is to name a goddess he cannot control.

Gloss: “Fiery,” “Scorch,” “Dawn” and “Flame.”
Sense: Four names that are nothing but description — and Phaethon still cannot remember them (193).
She opens the gates herself; the epithet supplies the dramatic irony.

Gloss: Latin Triones, the plough-oxen — Ursa Major read as a wagon team.
A northern constellation figured as a ploughman.
Merops, Clymene's mortal husband and Phaethon's putative father.
Sense: The name he refused at 1.764 is the one he now longs for.

Gloss: Latin Luna; Ovid uses Luna, Phoebe and Diana for one goddess.
A river of Mygdonia in Thrace. The Latin is Mygdonius Melas, “the Mygdonian Melas”; melas is Greek for black.
Sense: Not attested elsewhere as a name for the Melas, and Soucy gives it no note. The line needs a monosyllable to close on, which “Melas” is not.

Gloss: Dis and Proserpina, unnamed.
An old sea-god, father of the Nereids.
Sense: At 1.187 the name stood for the sea; here he is a person who hides in a cave.

Gloss: Latin alma Tellus, “nourishing.”

Sense: Earth pleads for the sea by naming its god only as Jupiter's relation — the same move as 1.275.

Epithet: Atlas ... scarce shouldering the glowing vault

Gloss: The unformed mass of 1.8.
Latin pater omnipotens.

Sense: He is named by the job only at the instant he is killed for it.

Gloss: A western river, taken for the Po.
“Daughters of Helios” — Clymene's daughters, Phaethon's sisters.
Latin squalidus, unwashed and unkempt in mourning.
Sense: Grief rendered as a lapse of grooming, for the god whose whole business is brightness.

Gloss: The nominative Latin name.
Latin omnipotens.
Feminine of Phoibos; also the moon itself.
Guardian of the three-way crossroads (Latin trivia).

Sense: Jupiter's disguise: he rapes Callisto wearing the face of the goddess she serves.

Gloss: Daughter of Saturn.
A Cretan hunting goddess, here syncretized with Diana.
The Sun's; Diana and Apollo are twins.
“The Parrhasian girl” — Parrhasia, a district of Arcadia.
Born on Mount Cynthus, on Delos.
Sense: Four names in fifty lines — Phoebe, Trivia, Dictynna, Cynthia — one for each way of being the same goddess.

Gloss: Latin Tonantis coniunx.
Sense: She is named by the husband whose affair she is about to punish.

Gloss: Latin paelex, the same word used of Io at 1.726.

Sense: Juno's word for the woman Jupiter raped.

Gloss: Callisto is the daughter of the Lycaon of Book 1.
Sense: Book 1's wolf turns out to be her father — “she feared wolves, though her father then was one” (495).

Epithet: the old Ocean, whom the gods revere

Gloss: Latin regina deorum.
Sister of Phoroneus, an early king of Argos.
Sense: The same formation as Phoronis at 1.669, and Juno's proof that Jupiter restores the women he ruins.

Gloss: Latin garrule.
Sense: Addressed in the second person, and convicted by the epithet before the story starts.

Gloss: Larissa, a city of Thessaly.
Latin Delphicus; Delphi is his oracle.
A standing Greek name for Athena, of disputed sense.
Born of Vulcan's seed and the earth, without a mother.
Half man, half serpent — the first king of Athens.
The Latin name.
Nyctimene, turned owl for her incest.

Epithet: born to famed Coroneus of Phocis
made fowl for her foul sins

Sense: Ovid switches to this name at the moment Apollo kills the woman it refers to.

Gloss: Apollo as god of medicine, as at 1.523.
Sense: The healer's art fails him again, and this time he is the one who caused the wound.

Gloss: Half man, half horse; the same phrase used of Cecrops at 555.
Latin semifer, “half-beast.”
“Swift-flowing,” for the stream she was born beside.
Sense: Named for a river, and turned into a mare — neither the name nor the shape is hers to keep.

Gloss: Apollo's father, so the child's grandfather.
Sense: The thunderbolt is named by the family tie of the man it will kill.

Gloss: The three Parcae, who spin, measure and cut.
Philyra, an Oceanid, bore Chiron to Saturn.
Maia, one of the Pleiades.
Sense: At 1.670 Ovid gave the mother as a star; here he spells the descent out in full.

Gloss: Mercury's address to him.
Latin Atlantiades.
Latin index; the stone still carries the name.
Sense: He is punished into the thing he was — a stone that tells.

Gloss: The herald's staff of 1.672.
Born on Mount Cyllene in Arcadia.
The moon, named by the goddess.
The Latin name, used once in Book 2.
Sense: Ovid gives him nine other names and this one only when a mortal asks for it outright.

Epithet: born unto Atlas' child with Pleione
Gloss: Maia, daughter of Atlas and Pleione.
Sense: His own answer to that question — a genealogy where a name was asked for.

Gloss: Latin flava.
His father Vulcan kept his forge on Lemnos.
Latin Invidia, personified.
Born near Lake Triton in Libya.
Jupiter's address, while sending him to procure Europa.

Epithet: the lord and father of the gods, who wields the tri-forked flame, whose nods shake earth
Sense: Ovid piles up the full imperial titulature in the two lines before Jupiter turns himself into a bull.

Gloss: Agenor, king of Tyre.
Latin praeda, “plunder.”
Sense: The last word on her in Book 2 is a word for property.
